## Programs follow rules; learners find them. {.center .inverse background-color="#1F4257"}

::: {.notes}
Cover cap. 1 — 25 min totali.

- Titolo = sei-parole: `rules` cambia ruolo (input nel software classico, output dal learner). Il capitolo in 6 parole.
- Esercizi in coda: 4 formativi + 1 sommativo (T/E/paradigma in aula, P come sfida da casa) negli ultimi 8′.
:::

<!-- BEAT 1 — Hook visivo -->

## *The algorithm says discharge. It won't say why.*

![](../img/storyboard/sb-01_01.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

::: {.notes}
Lasciate la slide 3-5s muta: l'immagine fa il lavoro.

- Elena: risk score raccomanda dimissione di cui dubita, nessuno sa *perché*.
- Punto-chiave: l'antagonista del corso è l'**opacità**, non l'algoritmo.
:::

<!-- BEAT 2 — Contesto (the input/output swap) -->

## *You write the rules. A learner finds them.*

![](../img/storyboard/sb-01_02.png){fig-align="center" width="78%"}

::: {.notes}
Voce: software classico = voi scrivete le regole + date i dati. ML = date dati *e* risposte, la macchina restituisce la **regola**. Inversione input/output.
:::

## Two ways of writing software

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Traditional programming**

- you write the **rules** (algorithm)
- you provide **input** data
- you obtain the **answer**
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Machine learning**

- you provide **training input** (data)
- you provide **training answers** (labels)
- you obtain the **rule** itself: $Y \simeq f(X)$
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Stessi blocchi, frecce invertite: l'algoritmo è *output*. La $f$ in $Y \simeq f(X)$ si impara dal training.

Take-away (a voce): il ML è **ottimizzazione**, non programmazione esplicita.
:::

## ML vs traditional programming — at a glance

![](../img/MLvsTrad.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

::: {.notes}
A voce: dove entrano i dati, dove escono le regole.

Citare Samuel (1959): *"algorithms that give computers the capability to learn without being explicitly programmed"*.
:::

<!-- BEAT 3 — Sfida / Dati (accuracy trap) -->

## *95% accurate — and clinically useless.*

![](../img/storyboard/sb-01_03.png){fig-align="center" width="78%"}

::: {.notes}
Punto: su esito raro (5%) il "sempre-negativo" fa 95% accuracy senza prendere un caso. L'accuracy inganna.

- A voce: in clinica l'esito che conta è quasi sempre lo sbilanciato.
- Gancio al beat 4: lo riprendiamo definendo $P$.
:::

## Warning: unbalanced data need balanced metrics

- **Accuracy** = $\dfrac{\text{correctly classified}}{\text{total}}$
- On rare outcomes ($\sim 5\%$) the *trivial* "always-negative" classifier scores ~$95\%$ accuracy and misses every real case.
- We will need *other* measures (and other procedures — chapter 04) to do better.

::: {.notes}
Qui solo seminare: *accuracy non basta*. Le metriche (sens/spec, AUC, balanced acc) NON si insegnano ora → gancio al cap. 04.

Il sommativo finale li costringe a *scegliere* una $P$ per scenario.
:::

<!-- BEAT 4 — Nodo / Impatto: T, P, E -->

## *Task · Performance · Experience: that's the whole machine.*

![](../img/storyboard/sb-01_04.png){fig-align="center" width="72%"}

::: {.notes}
Mitchell 1997. Tre coordinate: $T$ compito, $P$ misura, $E$ dati.

Punto da far atterrare: nominare $T/P/E$ di un sistema = metà del lavoro per giudicarlo.
:::

## Mitchell's definition

> *"A computer program is said to **learn** from **experience** ($E$) with respect to some class of **tasks** ($T$) and **performance measure** ($P$), if its performance at tasks in $T$, as measured by $P$, improves with experience $E$."*
>
> — Tom Mitchell, *Machine Learning*, 1997

![](../img/Tom-Mitchell-2.webp){fig-align="center" width="22%"}

::: {.notes}
Punto: learning = $P$ su $T$ migliora al crescere di $E$. **Non** "diventare intelligente": è un numero che sale.
:::

## $T$ — the task

| Learning problem | Task **$T$** |
|---|---|
| Predict 30-day readmission | classify patients as *will / will-not* be re-admitted |
| Handwriting recognition | recognise / classify handwritten characters in images |
| Self-driving car | drive from A to B |
| Disease coding from EHR | classify EHR notes by reported disease |
| In-bed patient monitoring | output position + dynamics at any given time |

::: {.notes}
Distinzione a voce: il task è *cosa* fa su un nuovo input, **non** il training. Il training produce il modello; il task è del problema, non del processo.
:::

## $P$ — the performance measure

| Task **$T$** | Performance **$P$** |
|---|---|
| classify readmission yes/no | $\%$ correctly classified (balanced! — class imbalance) |
| classify handwritten characters | $\%$ correctly classified |
| drive A → B | average distance before a human-judged error |
| classify EHR by disease | $\%$ of EHRs correctly classified |
| monitor in-bed dynamics | average error on position / dynamics |

::: {.notes}
$P$ = un *numero*, compatibile con output e distribuzione delle classi.

Richiamo beat 3: su esiti rari "$\%$ correctly classified" non basta (95% trivial-accuracy).
:::

## $E$ — the experience (the data)

| Task **$T$** | Experience **$E$** |
|---|---|
| classify readmission | EHR records with *known* re-admission outcomes |
| recognise handwriting | labelled images of handwritten characters |
| drive A → B | sequence of videos + steering commands from human drivers |
| classify EHR by disease | EHR notes with *known* disease labels |
| monitor in-bed dynamics | time-series from wearables + bed sensors + ground-truth video |

::: {.notes}
$E$ = i *dati* visti. La sua struttura (etichettato? sequenziale? interattivo?) determina il **tipo di apprendimento** → gancio al prossimo beat.

Aside: $E$ pre-esistente (training set) vs $E$ generata dall'interazione (RL).
:::

<!-- BEAT 5 — Metodo / Soluzione: where do labels come from? -->

## *Where do the labels come from?*

![](../img/storyboard/sb-01_05.png){fig-align="center" width="76%"}

::: {.notes}
Domanda-chiave che smista i 4 tipi. È anche la chiave del sommativo: *dove sono le label e quando arrivano* → paradigma.
:::

## Four kinds, in box order

- **Supervised** *(tag)* — inputs come **with** their correct outputs (the *labels*); the model learns from its errors on them.
- **Unsupervised** *(pattern)* — input data has **no labels**; the model finds *patterns* / clusters on its own.
- **Active** *(raised hand)* — the model *queries an oracle* (e.g., a clinician) to label the cases it is **most uncertain about**.
- **Reinforcement** *(trophy)* — an *agent* takes actions and receives *rewards*; it learns a policy that maximises long-term gain.

::: {.notes}
Ricucire alle 4 icone della slide precedente (da sinistra): tag → supervised, pattern → unsupervised, mano alzata → active, trofeo → reinforcement.

Aside da far atterrare: nessuno è "meglio" — dipende dal problema.
:::

<!-- BEAT 6 — Payoff / Domanda finale -->

## *You know what it is. But how does it decide?*

![](../img/storyboard/sb-01_06.png){fig-align="center" width="78%"}

::: {.notes}
Elena ora sa **cos'è** ($T/P/E$) e che **tipo** di apprendimento. Ma non *come* decide → gancio al cap. 2.
:::

## Pre-hook → chapter 2: classifiers

The simplest learner makes **one** decision: it draws a line on a chart of features and asks *which side* a patient falls on.

That line-drawer is a **classifier** — and it is where the black box opens next.

::: {.notes}
Pre-hook scriptato. 30s sul "*draws a line*" = gancio al riquadro 1 dello storyboard cap. 02.

**Non rivelare** il vocabolario ($f:\mathbb{R}^d \to \{1,\ldots,K\}$, partizione, 0/1 loss): lasciare la *domanda* aperta.
:::

<!-- ---------------- Item 01 — MCQ — ML vs traditional programming -->

## Item 01 — Question

A hospital deploys a model that predicts 30-day readmission from each patient's EHR. **Which statement best captures how this machine-learning system differs from a traditional, rule-based program written for the same task?**

- **A)** In traditional programming an engineer writes the decision rules and the program applies them to data; in machine learning the rules — the model — are *learned* from data paired with known outcomes.
- **B)** Machine learning needs no data, whereas a traditional program requires data as input.
- **C)** A traditional program can only handle numeric inputs, while machine learning is the only approach able to process patient records at all.
- **D)** Machine learning is guaranteed to be more accurate than any hand-written rule, because learning from data removes human bias.

::: {.notes}
Item 01 — MCQ Comprehension, low–medium. Obj. 2 (ML vs programmazione tradizionale). ~60s.

Ref: `course/01-introduction/items/item_01_ml-vs-programming_mcq.md`.
:::

## Item 01 — Solution (write yours)

::: {.notes}
Slide bianca. 60-90s per scegliere A/B/C/D, poi accolgo l'opzione più votata e la giustifico. Avanzo al consenso.
:::

## Item 01 — Solution

**Correct: A.** The defining difference is the **input/output swap**. In ordinary software the rules are the *input* (hand-written) and answers come out; in ML you provide the data *and* the known answers, and the model — the rule $Y \simeq f(X)$ — is the *output*, learned from training data.

Why the distractors are wrong:

- **B** inverts the dependency: ML is *more* data-dependent, not less.
- **C** is a false capability claim: rule-based programs can process records too; data type is not what distinguishes the two approaches.
- **D** is the "ML is objective / always better" misconception: a model can score 95% accuracy and still be clinically useless on imbalanced data, and it inherits whatever bias is in its training data.

::: {.notes}
Rinforza beat 2. Se scelgono D → gancio all'accuracy trap del beat 3 (95% trivial-accuracy).
:::

<!-- ---------------- Item 02 — Applicativa — T/P/E + balanced accuracy -->

## Item 02 — Question

An ICU team wants a system that, **at admission**, predicts whether a patient will develop **sepsis during their ICU stay**. They have several years of past ICU admissions, each described by the information available *at admission* and labelled with whether sepsis later occurred. In their data, only about **4% of admissions developed sepsis**.

1. Frame this as a machine-learning problem by specifying its **Task ($T$)**, **Performance measure ($P$)**, and **Experience ($E$)**.

2. **Balanced accuracy** = average of the model's accuracy *within each class*.
   Consider a trivial model that predicts "no sepsis" for every patient.
   *(a)* What is its plain accuracy, and its balanced accuracy?
   *(b)* Use your answer to explain why balanced accuracy is the more appropriate choice of $P$.

::: {.notes}
Item 02 — Application open-ended, medium. Obj. 1 ($T/P/E$ + scelta di $P$). ~4 min live (calcoli inclusi); di norma homework, in aula solo discussione.

Ref: `items/item_02_tpe-framing_applicativa.md`, rubrica `rubriche/rubrica_02_tpe-framing.md`.
:::

## Item 02 — Solution (write yours)

::: {.notes}
Slide bianca: scrivo $T/P/E$ + i numeri-chiave **96% / 50%**. Se già fatto a casa, raccolgo a voce; altrimenti 4 min.
:::

## Item 02 — Solution

**Framing**

- **$T$:** predict, at admission, whether a patient will develop sepsis during the ICU stay — *binary classification*.
- **$P$:** **balanced accuracy** (rather than plain accuracy).
- **$E$:** past ICU admissions labelled with whether sepsis occurred — *supervised* experience.

**The revealing computation**

- *(a)* "Always no-sepsis" model: correct on 96% of patients ⇒ **plain accuracy ≈ 96%**.
  Accuracy on sepsis class = $0\%$; on non-sepsis = $100\%$. ⇒ **Balanced accuracy = (0% + 100%) / 2 = 50%**.
- *(b)* Plain accuracy is inflated by the 96% majority of negatives, so a clinically useless model still scores ≈ 96%. Balanced accuracy weighs the two classes equally; missing the rare class drags it to chance (50%) — honestly revealing the model is useless for the task that matters.

::: {.notes}
Grading: balanced accuracy è definita nell'enunciato → valutare il *ragionamento*, non il vocabolario. "50% = no better than chance" con altre parole = già *Good*.

Rubrica: `rubriche/rubrica_02_tpe-framing.md`.
:::

<!-- ---------------- Item 03 — MCQ — Learning paradigm -->

## Item 03 — Question

A team builds a model that classifies chest X-rays as *normal* or *abnormal*. Labelling is expensive, so: they train the model on a small set of already-labelled X-rays, then let it scan many *unlabelled* X-rays and **select the few it is most uncertain about**; a radiologist labels only those, the model is retrained, and the cycle repeats.

**Which learning paradigm best describes this set-up?**

- **A)** Supervised learning, because the model is ultimately trained on radiologist-labelled X-rays.
- **B)** Active learning, because the model repeatedly queries an expert (the oracle) to label the cases it is most uncertain about.
- **C)** Reinforcement learning, because the model improves over repeated cycles by interacting with its environment.
- **D)** Unsupervised learning, because the model scans many X-rays that have no labels.

::: {.notes}
Item 03 — scenario MCQ, medium. Obj. 3 (paradigma). Distrattore seducente: **A** (underlying model *è* supervised); discriminante = *richiesta selettiva* di label all'oracolo.

Ref: `items/item_03_learning-paradigm_mcq.md`.
:::

## Item 03 — Solution (write yours)

::: {.notes}
Slide bianca. Se c'è tempo, poll Slido a 4 opzioni; se vince A → momento perfetto per insegnare *active vs supervised*.
:::

## Item 03 — Solution

**Correct: B — Active learning.**

The defining feature is the loop in which the model itself *chooses* which unlabelled cases to send to a human oracle for labelling — selective querying *is* active learning.

Why the distractors are plausible but wrong:

- **A** — the underlying model *is* a supervised classifier, but "supervised" alone misses what distinguishes the scenario: the model's *selective request* for labels. Active learning is a strategy built *on top of* supervised learning.
- **C** — confuses "repeated cycles" with reinforcement learning. RL requires a *reward* signal guiding actions; here there is no reward, only requested labels.
- **D** — many X-rays *are* unlabelled, but the model is trained on labels (just sparingly requested), so it is not unsupervised.

::: {.notes}
Take-away: active = supervised + scelta delle label da richiedere. Se serve, link allo scenario D del sommativo (disease coding): stesso schema.
:::

<!-- ---------------- Item 04 — Argomentativa — Critique a framing -->

## Item 04 — Question

A hospital data team is asked to **discover, from routinely collected lab panels, previously unrecognised subgroups ("phenotypes")** of patients with type 2 diabetes — groups nobody has defined in advance.

A colleague argues: *"We already have each patient's ICD diagnostic codes — let's just use those codes as the group labels and train a supervised classifier."*

1. **Argue** whether using the ICD codes as labels actually achieves the stated goal.
2. **State which learning paradigm fits the goal**, and justify it.
3. Under what (different) goal would the colleague's supervised approach be exactly the right choice?

::: {.notes}
Item 04 — Argumentation, medium–high. Obj. 3 + 1. ~3 min live; di norma **homework argomentativo**, in aula proietto la solution.

Ref: `items/item_04_critique-framing_argomentativa.md`, rubrica `rubriche/rubrica_04_critique-framing.md`.
:::

## Item 04 — Solution (write yours)

::: {.notes}
Slide bianca: costruisco l'argomentazione a 3 punti alla lavagna, mostrando lo **swap di obiettivo** (predire ICD esistente vs scoprire fenotipi nuovi). Senza tempo → salto alla solution.
:::

## Item 04 — Solution

1. **The ICD-codes proposal does *not* achieve the goal.** ICD codes are *pre-existing, human-defined* diagnostic categories — not the *previously unrecognised* subgroups the task asks to discover. A supervised classifier trained on them would only learn to reproduce labels that already exist; it cannot surface new structure.
   **"Labels available" ≠ "labels that match the goal."**

2. **Unsupervised learning (clustering)** fits the goal: discover structure / subgroups in data that carry *no* labels for the thing being sought (the phenotypes).

3. The colleague's **supervised** approach would be exactly right under a *different* goal: **predicting a patient's existing ICD diagnosis from their lab panels.** There the ICD codes are legitimately the target labels, and assigning new patients to known categories is supervised classification.

::: {.notes}
Payoff: separare *goal vs availability of labels*. Grading: premiare la coerenza, non le keyword ("clustering"/"unsupervised"/equivalenti valgono uguale).

Rubrica: `rubriche/rubrica_04_critique-framing.md`.
:::

## Summative — *Turn a clinical problem into an ML problem* {.inverse .smaller background-color="#1F4257"}

For each scenario, write its **Task ($T$)**, **Experience ($E$)** and the **learning paradigm**.

- **A — 30-day readmission.** Flag, at discharge, which inpatients will be re-admitted within 30 days from EHR.
- **B — Patient phenotypes.** From lab panels of diabetic patients, find data-driven subgroups *not* predefined.
- **C — Adaptive insulin dosing.** A controller adjusts each insulin dose from the patient's glucose response over time.
- **D — Disease coding from free text.** Classify EHR notes by disease; the model asks the clinician to label the cases it is most uncertain about.

*Take-home challenge:* propose a quantitative **performance measure $P$** for each — we'll revisit at chapter 4 (model validation).

::: {.notes}
**Sommativo** — ultimi ~8′. Chiedo solo $T$, $E$, paradigma; la $P$ è prematura (cap. 4) → la sfida da casa su $P$ è il gancio al cap. 4.

- Paradigmi: A supervised, B unsupervised, C reinforcement, D active.
- Spotlight nel reveal sui controintuitivi **C e D**; A/B si auto-correggono via poll Slido.
- Duale: unica tabella condivisa a 4 righe (remoto + presenza convergono).
- Classe piccola: distribuisco A/B/C, tengo D come reveal collettivo.
:::

## Summative — Solution (write yours)

::: {.notes}
Slide bianca: riempio la tabella a 4 righe in tempo reale mentre riportano. Success criterion: ≥ 3 of 4 rows correct on first pass.
:::

## Summative — Solution {.smaller}

| | $T$ (task) | $E$ (experience) | Paradigm |
|:-:|:--|:--|:-:|
| **A** | Discharge: readmitted yes/no | EHRs with outcome labels | **supervised** |
| **B** | Find subgroups in lab panels | Lab panels, **no** labels | **unsupervised** |
| **C** | Insulin dose from glucose state | State → action → response stream | **reinforcement** |
| **D** | Classify EHR notes by disease | Notes + labels on asked-for cases | **active** |

::: {.notes}
Reveal per insegnare, non penalizzare:

- **C:** in RL $E$ NON è dataset etichettato ma *stream* di interazioni → accetto se nomina interazione/feedback sequenziale.
- **D:** "supervised" non è del tutto sbagliato (model *è* supervised); preciso = "active" per la **richiesta selettiva di label**.
- Take-home: $P$ rivista al cap. 4 (model selection & validation).
:::
